coverage.method: Complete page-by-page extracted text read; rendered pages separately listed where inspected.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Stability and preservation of revolutionary gains
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Doyle presents a constituency that valued equality and property gains but tired of war and political mobilization. Enduring settlement required calm; Bonaparte’s success involved sacrificing many 1789 principles, not straightforward fulfillment of all of them.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: stability; revolutionary gains; political fatigue; end of Revolution
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Retain difference between property/equality beneficiaries and approval of every revolutionary regime.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Voters rejected endorsed candidates despite very low participation; Councils largely accepted majority returns and then purged the Directory. Sieyès used cross-faction constitutional resentment to concentrate executive power, contrary to some supporters’ expectations.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Year VII elections; Prairial coup 1799; Sieyès; Treilhard; Directors
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Distinguish this Prairial from 1795 and legislative purge of executive from earlier reverse coups.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Manège and a revived press accompanied full conscription, forced loan and Law of Hostages. The last allowed sanctions against relatives without proven complicity. Memories of Year II helped Sieyès and Fouché suppress the revival.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Manège Club; Jourdan; forced loan; Law of Hostages; Fouché
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Keep measures distinct and describe resemblance to Terror as political perception as well as concrete coercive power.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Toulouse resisted a royalist peasant rising while Sieyès suppressed the left. Jourdan’s country-in-danger motion failed. Allied divisions enabled victories in Holland/Switzerland; western chouannerie resumed amid conscription anxiety.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Toulouse rising; Country in Danger motion; Brune; Daendels; chouan revival
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Do not imply every threat was Jacobin or that successful republican defence made emergency power universally accepted.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Brumaire coup and coalition of conspirators
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Sieyès needed a general for extra-constitutional change; Bonaparte exploited the opportunity. Lucien, Fouché and Talleyrand helped. Removal to Saint-Cloud, executive collapse, legislative resistance and military expulsion preceded provisional consuls.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: 18 Brumaire; Saint-Cloud; Lucien Bonaparte; provisional Consulate
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve agency, pretext versus proven plot and improvised coercion; source date discrepancy noted.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Directory failure: political culture versus constitutional diagnosis
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Doyle argues elections never operated freely and rulers failed to accept legitimate parties/opposition, but also recognizes opponents’ restoration aims or terroristic rhetoric and likely intolerance. Bonaparte and Sieyès proposed different executive remedies.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Directory failure; party politics; general will; opposition legitimacy; electoral sovereignty
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Retain balanced qualification; do not reduce causal explanation to a mechanically weak executive.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Year VIII constitution and truncated representation
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Tiered lists selected eligible citizens; Senate chose legislators. Tribunate debated without voting, Legislative Body voted without debate, and only government initiated laws via Council of State. Bonaparte rejected Sieyès’s Grand Elector plan for dominant First Consul power.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Year VIII constitution; Senate; Tribunate; Legislative Body; Council of State; Grand Elector
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Review each power/direction and distinguish proposed from adopted institutions.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Constitutional plebiscite and claimed end of Revolution
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Approval figures were inflated amid large abstention and implementation preceded the result. Official claims to preserve original principles are not Doyle’s unqualified evaluation; stability remained to be achieved.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Year VIII plebiscite; constitutional legitimacy; end of Revolution proclamation
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Do not convert official declaration into author-endorsed factual completion on proclamation date.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Victorious peace and the Consulate’s security
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Russian withdrawal weakened the coalition. Marengo narrowly escaped defeat; Moreau’s Hohenlinden victory forced peace. Lunéville and Amiens consolidated gains while colonial and commercial concessions differed. These settlements were central to domestic legitimacy.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Marengo; Hohenlinden; Lunéville; Amiens; Moreau; Russian withdrawal
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve distinct generals and decisive roles; do not attribute all victory to Bonaparte or make peace permanent.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Pragmatic settlement with monarchies and client territories
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Etruria’s Bourbon kingdom, recognition of Naples and Spanish cession of Louisiana show altered regime priorities; Parthenopean restoration was abandoned. France could exact more from allies than enemies.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Etruria; Naples settlement; Louisiana; Spain; satellite states
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Distinguish restoration of monarchy from general restoration of pre-revolutionary arrangements.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: British naval victories, Malta, armed neutrality and Copenhagen left sea power intact but could not reverse French continental domination. War weariness and political change made Amiens possible on strongly French-favouring terms.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Britain; Malta; armed neutrality; Copenhagen; Pitt resignation; Addington; Amiens
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Keep military strength at sea separate from negotiating success and transient peace.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Some hoped Bonaparte would act as a French Monck. He delayed rejecting Louis XVIII, pacified chouan leaders through conciliation and coercion, then guaranteed revolutionary property while allowing émigré return. Cadoudal remained hostile.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Louis XVIII overtures; royalist hopes; chouan pacification; émigré amnesty; national lands
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Distinguish strategic ambiguity from commitment to Bourbon restoration and legal text from practical amnesty.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Infernal machine and deliberate anti-Jacobin repression
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Cadoudal’s chouans caused the bombing, yet Bonaparte used it against Jacobins despite police proof. Deportations and executions also aimed to reassure property owners.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: infernal machine; Cadoudal; Fouché; Jacobin repression; Seychelles deportation
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Exact culpability and the instrumental use of a false attribution are crucial stance/access distinctions.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Repeal of coercive laws, Bank of France, cash debt service, tax collection, prefects and special courts projected stability. Conscription evasion fed brigandage; returning troops enabled suppression. A Civil Code drew on older projects and clarified property law.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Bank of France; prefects; brigandage/chauffeurs; special courts; Civil Code; tax recovery
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve earlier foundations and provisional financial strength; distinguish everyday legality from high-level contempt for legal procedure.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Church-state conflict had broken early consensus. Bonaparte regarded religion pragmatically as support for order, while Pius VII’s accommodation of equality made negotiation possible. Reconciliation could separate religious allegiance from counter-revolution.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Bonaparte religion; Pius VII; religious reconciliation; Concordat negotiations
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Do not infer personal faith from strategic religious gestures or treat settlement as unilateral papal submission.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Catholicism was recognized as majority religion with freedom of worship retained; bishops were state-nominated and papally invested, clergy publicly supported and obedient. Church lands were not restored, though papal acceptance did not concede legality of confiscation.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Concordat; Catholic majority/state church; episcopal appointment; church lands; freedom of worship
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve distinction between majority status and exclusive state religion, temporal nomination and spiritual authority.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Ecclesiastical reconstitution, papal power and Organic Articles
findings.source_grounded_analysis: All old bishops were displaced; Tam multa and papal deprivation expanded recognized authority. Some constitutional bishops returned. Unilateral Organic Articles restricted papal communication and revived Gallican teaching, producing a mixed settlement rather than simple ultramontane victory.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Tam multa; constitutional/refractory bishops; Organic Articles; Gallican Articles; papacy
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Keep resignation, deprivation and appointment mechanisms distinct; reconcile increased papal recognition with state restrictions.

findings.source_grounded_analysis: Experienced nominated legislators still criticized policy. Senate removal of opponents used ambiguous renewal provisions before Concordat enactment; independent press loss limits public-reaction evidence. Consul for life and Easter celebrations marked stability secured at representative freedom’s expense.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Tribunate purge; Legislative Body purge; Daunou; Consul for life; Easter1802; Law on Cults
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Keep police-reported opinion qualified and source year discrepancy explicit; distinguish public celebration from universal consent.

uncertainties.issue: Narrative begins coup on 9 November, calls next day 18 Brumaire on p375, and gives Elders speech as10 November on p376. Preserve internal calendar/date problem rather than silently correcting source.
p389 calls legislative purge January1801, but describes November1801 session and YearX renewal before April1802 Concordat. Preserve source chronology inconsistency.
